name: Synthetic Portraiture
title: Synthetic Portraiture
answer: Synthetic portraiture is the creation of photographic-style likenesses of people who do not exist, or the re-rendering of real people in new poses, lighting, and settings. It sits between portrait photography and hyper-realist painting, but the output is produced by generative models rather than a camera or brush. Practitioners work with prompts, reference images, and post-processing to produce headshots, editorial portraits, and character studies. The field includes both fully fictional faces and the licensed or consented recreation of real individuals. This site tracks 1,000 live image generation models, many of which are used for this kind of work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most synthetic portraiture runs on cloud-hosted diffusion models or local GPU workstations with consumer or professional graphics cards. The models are typically text-to-image or image-to-image systems accessed through APIs, desktop apps, or open source pipelines. Training and fine-tuning require more substantial hardware, but day-to-day generation can often be done on a single modern GPU. Storage and versioning matter because portrait datasets and model checkpoints are large and frequently updated.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners usually begin with a text prompt describing age, expression, lighting, lens, and background, then iterate through generated candidates. They may use inpainting to fix eyes, teeth, hair, or hands, and outpainting to extend a frame. Reference images and control nets allow a pose or composition to be held steady while the face or style changes. Final images are often retouched in standard photo editing software to remove artifacts and match color grading.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Synthetic portraiture raises questions about likeness rights, consent, and disclosure. Using a real person's face without permission can violate publicity rights or privacy rules, even if the output is not a photograph. Many professional settings now require clear labeling when an image is AI-generated, and some stock and client contracts demand proof of model training provenance. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a reminder that the legal boundaries around training data and likeness are still being settled. Practitioners typically keep records of prompts, seeds, model versions, and any reference images used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The trend is toward finer control over identity, expression, and lighting, with shorter generation times and better consistency across a series of portraits. Video portraits and real-time avatars are becoming more common, blurring the line between still photography and moving image. Watermarking and provenance standards are likely to become embedded in the tools themselves. As models improve, the skill will shift from fixing artifacts to directing subtle character and mood.
